nodes.label: Guerrini et al. (2001) described a pedigree in which 8 individuals had a nonprogressive disorder with onset between 12 and 50 years of age. All of them had mainly distal, semicontinuous rhythmic myoclonus and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and 3 had complex partial seizures. Most rarely had seizures and had normal cognition, but 3 individuals with intractable seizures had mild mental retardation. All patients had frontotemporal as well as generalized interictal EEG abnormalities.

Guerrini et al. (2001) found from neurophysiologic studies that the myoclonus was cortical in origin. In 5 patients, EEG over the contralateral rolandic area was coherent with EMG at 8 to 25 Hz, and EEG activity preceded EMG activity by 8 to 15 ms. Ipsilateral coherence in 2 patients was consistent with transcallosal spread. Patients had an enhanced C-reflex and high-amplitude somatosensory and visual evoked potentials. Compared with controls, they also had a reduced resting motor threshold to transcranial magnetic stimulation and a shortened post-MEP silent period. The authors suggested that these findings reflect diffuse cortical hyperexcitability.
Guerrini et al. (2001) found that inheritance in the ADCME family was autosomal dominant with high penetrance.

Guerrini et al. (2001) performed a genome-wide linkage analysis and identified a 12.4-cM critical region on 2p11.1-q12.2 between markers D2S2161 and D2S1897. The maximum 2-point lod score was 3.46 at theta = 0.0 for D2S2175, and the multipoint lod score reached 3.74 around D2S2175.

Guerrini et al. (2001) excluded linkage to the familial adult myoclonic epilepsy locus on 8q23.3-q24 in their family. Based on the new chromosome 2 localization and the different phenotype, they defined ADCME as a new epilepsy syndrome.

Labauge et al. (2002) described a 4-generation European family with 18 members and familial adult myoclonic epilepsy (FAME). Ten living and 3 deceased relatives were affected. In the 10 living patients, mean age at onset was 41 years (range, 30-60 years). Eight of the 13 affected individuals had generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Electrophysiologic studies in 5 patients confirmed the diagnosis of FAME.
In the European family studied by Labauge et al. (2002), the pattern of inheritance was consistent with autosomal dominant transmission.

Labauge et al. (2002) performed linkage analysis in the European FAME family using fluorescent microsatellites spanning the FAME/BAFME locus on 8q23.3-q24.1, and the locus was excluded. The authors concluded that this exclusion established genetic heterogeneity of the disorder. They also noted that the family extended the occurrence of FAME to non-Japanese patients.

de Falco et al. (2003) carried out a clinical and electrophysiologic study of 2 Italian families with benign adult familial myoclonic epilepsy (BAFME). Both families showed linkage to chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2.

de Falco et al. (2003) noted that BAFME had been mapped to chromosome 8q24. Their finding that 2 Italian families were linked to chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2 supported genetic heterogeneity and the existence of non-Japanese families with BAFME.
de Falco et al. (2003) suggested that BAFME linked to chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2 might be allelic with the recently described autosomal dominant cortical myoclonus and epilepsy (ADCME) syndrome.

Striano et al. (2005) reported a 5-generation family from Naples, Italy, with cortical tremor, myoclonus, and epilepsy. Eleven members, aged 24 to 56 years (mean, 39.2 years), had hand tremor and myoclonus, and 6 of them had generalized seizures. Electrophysiologic study confirmed cortical reflex myoclonus in all affected members.

In the family studied by Striano et al. (2005), 3 presymptomatic members had giant somatosensory evoked potential components and an enhanced long loop reflex I. After 1.5 years of follow-up, these members developed hand tremor and myoclonus of the upper limbs.
By linkage analysis of an Italian family with cortical tremor, myoclonus, and epilepsy, Striano et al. (2005) found significant linkage to chromosome 2p (maximum lod score of 5.9).
Saint-Martin et al. (2008) refined the 2p11.1-q12.2 locus responsible for cortical tremor associated with epilepsy and excluded candidate genes in the region.

Madia et al. (2008) genotyped 53 affected individuals from 5 southern Italian families with benign adult familial myoclonic epilepsy (BAFME), one not previously reported, using microsatellite markers spanning chromosomes 2p11.1-q12.2 and 8q23.1-q24.11. Multipoint linkage analysis found significant linkage to chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2, with a maximum cumulative lod score of 18.5 for markers D2S2161 and D2S388.

Madia et al. (2008) found that the haplotype '5332' of the adjacent markers D2S388, D2S2216, D2S113, and D2S2175 segregated with the disease in all 5 Italian BAFME families. They concluded that the same mutation, inherited from a common ancestor, segregates in these families, indicating a founder effect.

In a preliminary genotype-phenotype analysis, Madia et al. (2008) found only minor clinical differences among patients carrying the founder disease haplotype. They suggested that other factors do not markedly influence the expressivity of the founder mutation.

Madia et al. (2008) described benign adult familial myoclonic epilepsy (BAFME or FAME) as an autosomal dominant condition characterized by shivering-like tremors of cortical origin, myoclonus, and epilepsy.

Suppa et al. (2009) described an Italian family with familial cortical myoclonic tremor with epilepsy (FCMTE). Clinically affected family members had limb and voice tremor, seizures, and myoclonus of the eyelids during blinking. Neuropsychological testing showed visuospatial impairment, which the authors suggested may be due to temporal lobe dysfunction.
In the Italian FCMTE family, Suppa et al. (2009) found neurophysiologic evidence suggesting increased excitability of the primary motor cortex with normal sensorimotor integration.

In the Italian FCMTE family, Suppa et al. (2009) used linkage analysis to exclude the 8q24 locus. Affected members shared a common haplotype spanning 14.5 Mb in the region of chromosome 2 near the centromere.

Crompton et al. (2012) described a 6-generation kindred of European descent, ascertained in New Zealand and Australia, with familial adult myoclonic epilepsy. All 55 affected family members had fine hand tremor, usually beginning in adolescence (median age 15 years; range 4-60 years). Proximal myoclonus was present in 44 of 55 (80%) and began later than the hand tremor (median age 17 years; range 5-60 years). Generalized tonic-clonic seizures occurred in 8 of 55 (15%), with a median age at onset of 43.5 years (range 18-76 years).

Crompton et al. (2012) found on neurophysiologic testing that affected members of the family had features of cortical reflex myoclonus. They concluded that the most common phenotype in this family was a mild postural hand tremor resembling essential tremor, together with subtle proximal myoclonus. Generalized tonic-clonic seizures were uncommon and occurred around sleep onset after severe generalized myoclonus.

In a 6-generation kindred with familial adult myoclonic epilepsy, Crompton et al. (2012) used genetic mapping to narrow the FAME2 locus on chromosome 2 to a 13.3-Mb interval containing 99 known protein-coding genes.
Crompton et al. (2012) described familial adult myoclonic epilepsy as an autosomal dominant syndrome, and reported it in a 6-generation kindred.

De Fusco et al. (2014) described autosomal dominant cortical myoclonus and epilepsy (ADCME) as a familial disorder with cortical reflex myoclonus. It shows as action-induced shivering movements of the hands and jerking of the upper limbs, variably associated with focal and generalized tonic-clonic seizures of variable severity. A minority of patients have borderline or moderately impaired cognition, and myoclonus often worsens in advanced age.

De Fusco et al. (2014) described a 4-generation Tuscan family (family B) with 5 affected members. All had postural myoclonus of the hands and upper limbs, and cortical tremor was the presenting symptom, starting between ages 18 and 50 years. All but one (IV:1) had epilepsy with rare generalized tonic-clonic seizures, at times triggered by visual stimuli; 2 patients also had drug-resistant focal motor or complex partial seizures. One patient had borderline cognitive level and the others had normal intelligence. Jerk-locked back-averaged EEG, somatosensory evoked potentials, and long-loop reflex studies were consistent with cortical reflex myoclonus. Brain MRI was normal where performed.
De Fusco et al. (2014) found no cardiovascular disease on careful history in any of the ADCME patients. Two of the oldest ADRA2B mutation carriers developed age-related dementia.

In a 5-generation Tuscan family (family A) with ADCME previously mapped to chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2, De Fusco et al. (2014) used candidate gene sequencing to identify a heterozygous in-frame insertion/deletion in the ADRA2B gene (c.675_686delTGGTGGGGCTTTinsGTTTGGCAG; p.H225_L229delinsQFGR). The change replaces 5 amino acids (HGGAL) in the third intracellular loop with 4 new residues (QFGR). The indel segregated completely with the disease and was absent from 575 Tuscan controls, dbSNP, the Exome Variant Server, and 1000 Genomes. Targeted capture and next-generation sequencing of the critical region in 2 affected members found it to be the only relevant change.

De Fusco et al. (2014) found the same ADRA2B indel in a second Tuscan ADCME family (family B). Family histories showed no known kinship between the 2 families, but they shared the same disease haplotype across the entire chromosome 2 critical region, suggesting a common ancestor.

De Fusco et al. (2014) sequenced BAFME pedigrees from southern Italy that map to the ADCME locus and found no ADRA2B mutations; Southern blot excluded large insertions or deletions. The authors suggested that ADCME and BAFME/FAME may be classified as 2 distinct clinical entities, although they could not exclude variants in regulatory or noncoding regions.

De Fusco et al. (2014) found that the indel lies on the common ADRA2B allele with 12 consecutive glutamic acid residues, not on the less common polymorphic short allele that is associated with cardiovascular and metabolic risk.

In transfected HeLa cells, De Fusco et al. (2014) showed that both wildtype and mutant ADRA2B localized normally to the plasma membrane. In the presence of arrestin-3, both moved to endosomes after epinephrine stimulation, indicating that the mutation did not impair protein maturation or arrestin-dependent internalization. Molecular modeling predicted that the mutation changes the conformation of the third intracellular loop.

In co-immunoisolation assays in CosM6 cells, De Fusco et al. (2014) found that spinophilin bound similar amounts of wildtype and mutant ADRA2B after 5 minutes of epinephrine. By 10 minutes, binding to the mutant had fallen back to basal levels while binding to wildtype stayed elevated, suggesting that the mutant cannot form a stable complex with spinophilin.

In Xenopus oocytes, De Fusco et al. (2014) found that spinophilin significantly raised the EC50 for epinephrine-stimulated Ca(2+)-activated Cl- current with wildtype ADRA2B but not with the mutant receptor. They concluded that the mutant increases the intensity of Ca(2+) signaling. They proposed that the mutation has a gain-of-function effect by reducing the interaction with spinophilin, possibly leading to cortical hyperexcitability through impaired GABAergic inhibition.

Corbett et al. (2019) summarized the clinical features of 22 FAME families. The families were mainly Italian; others were Australian/New Zealand, Sephardic Jewish (Iraqi and Israeli), South African, French/Spanish, French, and Syrian. Patients had cortical myoclonic tremor and myoclonic and later generalized tonic-clonic seizures, with onset usually in the second to third decade. Expressivity varied within and between families, and the frequency of GTCS ranged from 15% to 100% across families. Some families also had focal seizures.

Corbett et al. (2019) described a large Australian/New Zealand family of European ancestry (Family 1) with 55 affected members. All 55 had myoclonus/cortical tremor, 8 (15%) had tonic-clonic seizures, and 2 (4%) had focal seizures. Mean age of onset was 18.6 years, with a range of 4 to 60 years.

Corbett et al. (2019) found evidence of anticipation in the large Australian/New Zealand FAME2 family. Median age of onset was 30 years in generation III (n = 6), 17 years in generation IV (n = 30), and 12 years in generation V (n = 16).

Corbett et al. (2019) analysed whole-genome sequencing data from affected members of 3 FAME families (Families 1, 3 and 19) using ExpansionHunter and exSTRa. In all FAME samples tested, they found an expansion of an ATTTT repeat together with an inserted ATTTC repeat within the first intron of STARD7. The ATTTC repeat was absent from WGS data on 69 controls.

nodes.label: Corbett et al. (2019) used a repeat-primed PCR assay and detected the STARD7 ATTTC expansion in all 137 affected individuals from 16 previously reported FAME2 families. It was also present in all 20 affected individuals from 6 additional multiplex families and in 1 of 52 unrelated singleton cases, giving 158 of 158 typically affected individuals from 22 families. Two individuals without a FAME diagnosis carried the expansion and were likely presymptomatic, and 8 of 13 individuals with an uncertain diagnosis were carriers. The expansion was not found in 28 controls.
STARD7 ATTTC repeat expansion in intron 1

Corbett et al. (2019) used long-read sequencing to show the repeat structure. In one patient from Family 1, a SMRT read contained 274 AAATG and 387 AAAAT repeats, while a nanopore read contained 345 AAATG and 390 AAAAT repeats; the authors suggested this reflected somatic variation. A patient from Family 5 had 588 AAATG and 340 AAAAT repeats, 4645 bp in total. The repeat structure on the forward strand was (AAATG)n[N](AAAAT)n.

Corbett et al. (2019) found the STARD7 ATTTC expansion in 2 families (Families 4 and 15) that carried the previously reported ADRA2B variant c.675_686delTGGTGGGGCTTTinsGTTTGGCAG. The authors stated that this strongly suggested the ADRA2B allele is not causative.

In patient-derived fibroblasts, Corbett et al. (2019) found that STARD7 mRNA levels (by qPCR and RNA-seq) and protein levels (by Western blot) were not altered. RNA-seq detected no reads containing ATTTC repeats. The authors suggested that the repeat sequence itself is pathogenic, independent of any effect on the encompassing gene.

Corbett et al. (2019) stated that the FAME2 locus is the most frequently linked region in Caucasian individuals with FAME. By contrast, chromosome 8 linkage has so far been limited to Asian individuals.

Corbett et al. (2019) found that the ATTTC repeat primer was diagnostic for FAME, with 100% sensitivity in all families with linkage or suggestive linkage to chromosome 2. The endogenous ATTTT repeat varied in length naturally and was not suitable for screening.
